name: Vienna
info: Vienna is a city on the Danube at the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods in Austria, begun as the Roman camp of Vindobona in the 1st century, later the seat of the Babenbergs and the Habsburgs and the capital of Austria.

facts.founded: The Romans set up the military camp of Vindobona in the 1st century CE; construction of the legionary camp began around 97 CE, and the name is a borrowing of a Celtic toponym.
facts.where: On the Danube at the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods, where the Alps meet the Pannonian Basin, in north-eastern Austria; the city is surrounded by Lower Austria.
facts.known: The Roman camp of Vindobona; the seat of the Babenbergs and Habsburgs; the sieges of 1529 and 1683; the Congress of Vienna of 1814 to 1815; the Ringstrasse; Red Vienna; the music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven; the university founded in 1365
facts.today: Vienna is the capital and most populous city of Austria and one of its nine states.

t: Vienna began as the Roman camp of Vindobona in the 1st century, became the seat of the Babenberg dukes in 1155 and passed to the Habsburgs in 1278, who made it the seat of the Holy Roman Emperors.

It withstood Ottoman attacks in 1529 and 1683, hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815, and in the later 19th century replaced its fortifications with the Ringstrasse as it grew to more than two million people.
After the end of Austria-Hungary in 1918 it was the capital of a republic, was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938, and was occupied by the four Allied powers until the Austrian State Treaty of 1955.
dyk: When King Richard the Lionheart was captured near Vienna in 1192, his ransom of 50,000 silver marks, about 10 to 12 tons of silver, paid for a mint and the city walls built around the year 1200.

sections.origins:
Vienna lies on the Danube at the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods, the north-eastern foothills of the Alps, where they give way to the Pannonian Basin. The area was inhabited by modern humans from the Upper Palaeolithic, and the name Vindobona, which comes from a Celtic language, suggests that people lived there before the Romans came. The earliest settlement of the inner city lay south of the meandering Danube.

In the 1st century the Romans set up the military camp of Vindobona in the province of Pannonia, on the site of today's city centre, with an adjoining civilian town to secure the borders of the empire. Construction of the legionary camp began around 97 CE, and it was occupied by Legio X Gemina. At its peak Vindobona had a population of around 15,000 and formed part of a trade and communications network across the empire. It was raised to the status of a municipium in 212. Even today the streets of the First District show where the camp placed its walls and moats. Marcus Aurelius may have died there in 180 during a campaign against the Marcomanni.

The German name Wien comes from the river Wien, not from Vindobona, and first appears in the Salzburg Annals, which note a battle at a place named Wenia in 881.
sections.growth:
Vienna was an important site of trade as early as the 11th century. In the Exchange of Mautern between the Bishop of Passau and Margrave Leopold IV it is mentioned as a Civitas for the first time, which points to a well-ordered settlement. In 1221 the city received the rights of a city and a staple right, which obliged all traders passing through to offer their goods there. The Viennese became middlemen in trade, with far-reaching connections along the Danube basin and to Venice, and Vienna became one of the most important cities of the Holy Roman Empire.

The Habsburg duke Rudolf IV, called the Founder, founded the University of Vienna in 1365 and began the Gothic nave of the Stephansdom. After the Ottoman siege of 1529 Vienna was made into a fortress with eleven bastions, a moat and an open glacis, and these works accounted for much of the building well into the 17th century. After 1683 the city became largely Baroque, with garden palaces such as the Belvedere and Schönbrunn built in the suburbs. It is estimated that 150,000 people lived there in 1724 and 200,000 in 1790. The first factories were built from that time, and after 1837 Vienna was the centre of the railway network.

In 1858 the fortifications were demolished and the Ringstrasse was built in their place. Its historicist buildings characterise the architecture of Vienna to this day. The period peaked in the World Exhibition of 1873, just before a stock market crash. Censuses from 1869 onwards showed a population of 2,031,000 in 1910.
sections.rulers:
In 976 the Margraviate of Ostarrîchi was given to the Babenberg family, and Vienna lay at its border with Hungary. In 1155 Margrave Henry II of Austria made Vienna his capital, and in 1156 Austria became a duchy in the Privilegium Minus, with Vienna the seat of all later dukes. Duke Leopold V captured King Richard the Lionheart near Vienna in 1192, and the ransom allowed the creation of a mint and the building of city walls.

In 1278 Rudolf I took control of the Austrian lands after defeating Ottokar II of Bohemia and began to establish Habsburg rule. In Vienna this took a long time, because partisans of Ottokar stayed strong and there were several uprisings against Albert I. Under the Luxembourg emperors Prague was the imperial residence and Vienna stood in its shadow. Vienna received its own bishop in 1469. In 1485 King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary and his Black Army conquered the city, which served as the capital of Hungary until 1490. After the Blood Judgment of Wiener Neustadt in 1522 the city stood under direct imperial control, and in 1556 it became the seat of the Holy Roman Emperor.

Vienna became the capital of the Austrian Empire in 1804, and then of Austria-Hungary after the compromise of 1867. In 1918 it became the capital of the Republic of German-Austria, and in 1919 of the First Republic of Austria.
sections.life:
Vienna became Protestant rather quickly in the 16th century and was then re-Catholicised. The Jesuits were brought to the city in 1551 and gained a large influence at court, and Melchior Khlesl, Bishop of Vienna from 1600, led the Counter-Reformation there. Jews were expelled from the city in 1421 and 1422 under Albert V, and in 1670 they were driven out of their ghetto of 50 years, after which Leopoldstadt became a place where many Jews lived. In 1783 Joseph II modernised the city administration and created the Magistrate, and he closed the graveyards within the city.

Vienna became a leading centre of music, from the age of Viennese Classicism through the early part of the 20th century. Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven worked there, and it was home to Schubert, Brahms, Bruckner, Mahler and Johann Strauss I and II. The first Viennese café was opened in 1685 by the Armenian businessman Johannes Diodato, and café culture flourished in the early 19th century. Around 1900 Vienna was a centre of the Jugendstil, with Otto Wagner and the Vienna Secession, and Sigmund Freud, the first psychoanalyst, lived there. Industrialisation and migration from other parts of the empire raised the population sharply, and around 1900 Vienna had the second-largest Czech population in the world after Prague.

Karl Lueger was the leading figure of city politics around 1900. He brought fresh water from the mountains by a new pipeline and created a belt of meadows and forests round the city, but his policy was coupled with an intense anti-Semitism, which had popular support.
sections.crises:
The first Ottoman siege came in 1529. The medieval walls barely held until epidemics and an early winter forced the Ottoman army to withdraw. In 1683 the new fortifications let the city hold out for two months, until the Ottoman army was defeated by an army led by the Polish king John III Sobieski. The Turkish Wars turned against the Ottomans after it. In 1679 the Great Plague struck, and nearly a third of the inhabitants are said to have died of bubonic plague.

In the Napoleonic Wars the French took the city in 1805 without a battle and in 1809 after heavy fire. The March Revolution of 1848 forced Metternich to resign. In July 1927 a riot broke out after three far-right paramilitary members were acquitted of killing two members of the Republikanischer Schutzbund, and the Palace of Justice was set on fire. Police killed at least 84 protesters, and five policemen also died. In February 1934, after Dollfuss had dissolved parliament and banned the Communist Party, civil war spread to Vienna, where socialists barricaded themselves in housing estates until the army shelled the Karl-Marx-Hof and the Schutzbund surrendered.

After the Anschluss of March 1938 Viennese Jews were harassed and plundered, and in November 1938 all synagogues and prayer houses were destroyed except the Stadttempel. Of almost 200,000 Jews in Vienna, around 120,000 were driven to emigrate and approximately 65,000 were killed. From 17 March 1944 there were 51 air raids, and around a third of the city centre was destroyed. The Red Army entered the city on 6 April 1945 and took it after several days of fighting.
sections.legacy:
The Congress of Vienna met from September 1814 to June 1815 and redrew the political map of Europe, and the social life around it moved Prince de Ligne to say that the congress dances but does not progress. The Ringstrasse and its buildings, the Baroque palaces and gardens and the historic centre remain the city's architectural ensemble, and the centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.

Between the wars the city's Social Democrats ran the municipality from 1919 to 1934, in the period called Red Vienna. In 1921 Vienna became a state of its own, separate from Lower Austria. Over 60,000 apartments were built in municipal housing blocks between 1925 and 1934, among them the Karl-Marx-Hof, and these Gemeindebauten still serve as affordable housing. In 1938 the city was enlarged by 91 municipalities to 1,224 km², and the enlargement was reversed in 1954.

After the war the four powers divided Vienna into sectors from September 1945, with the First District an international zone whose control passed monthly among them. The Austrian State Treaty was signed in May 1955 and came into force on 27 July 1955, and by October all soldiers had left. In the 1970s Vienna became an official seat of the United Nations, and the Vienna International Centre was built. Vienna is today the capital of Austria and a state in its own right.

summary: Vienna grew from the Roman camp of Vindobona into the seat of the Babenbergs and then the Habsburgs. It withstood Ottoman sieges in 1529 and 1683, hosted the Congress of Vienna, and is today the capital of Austria.
notes: START: the main article says construction of the legionary camp began around AD 97; the history article says only 1st century. I used 97 with circa true.

DISAGREEMENT, early Middle Ages: the main article says the city was abandoned for several centuries after the Huns invaded Pannonia; the history article says the camp remains were not deserted and a small settlement stayed, with 6th-century coins and graves. I left the question out of the text.

DISAGREEMENT, population peak: the history article gives 2,031,000 in 1910 as the all-time high; the main article says more than two million in 1910 but also refers to a reported peak in 1916. I used only the 1910 census figure.

DISAGREEMENT, imperial residence: the history article says Vienna became the seat of the Holy Roman Emperor in 1556 (the history article also says Vienna became capital after Albert II's election, undated, which I left out); the main article says residence of the Habsburg emperors from 1611 to 1740 and again from 1745. I used 1556 only.
Danube regulation: the history article puts it in the 1860s and the main article says unregulated until 1870; left out of the text.
Plague of 1679: the main article says nearly one-third of the inhabitants died; I wrote 'are said to have died'. The history article also names an epidemic of 1713; left out.
Air raids: the history article says raids began by 1943; the main article says 51 raids from 17 March 1944. I used the main article's figures.
Jews of Vienna: the main article says around 120,000 emigrated and approximately 65,000 were killed in one place and 130,000 fled in another. I used the first.
Destruction of synagogues in 1938: the history article says the synagogues were destroyed, the main article says all except the Stadttempel; I used the main article's wording.
Quotation of Prince de Ligne paraphrased from the history article; it is hedged by 'moved ... to say'.

Left out: Richard the Lionheart's excommunicated captor's death, the Schottenstift Irish monks, the Aromanian diaspora, Rothschild bank, espionage, demographics and religion figures from recent censuses, politics since 1945, culture lists, sport and cuisine (guide forbids or not history).
The mention of an 8 September date etc. is not used. 'Seat of the Aulic Council' left out. The Hungarian name Bécs and other names left out.
